meta.name: EC-Council Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH v12)
meta.notes: [initial author pass (scheduled-agent 2026-06-16): 12 questions covering the 9 CEH v12 modules (recon, scanning/sniffing, system hacking, malware, web/SQLi, wireless, DoS, cryptography, cloud/IoT). Correct positions spread 3/3/3/3 across the four option slots. Parallel option phrasing; distractors are plausible CEH-adjacent terms rather than throwaway wrong answers; explanations name each distractor to teach the differentiator.] | v1.1 (2026-07-03): +10 scenario questions — pass-the-hash/LAPS, SNMP default community, XSS+HttpOnly session theft, WPA2 handshake cracking, DMARC alignment, ARP poisoning/DAI, SSRF+IMDS, MD5-vs-KDF password storage, honeypots, exposed Docker API. Balanced correct positions.

questions.question: During an external assessment, a pentester wants to map open TCP ports on a target while avoiding a full three-way handshake that would be logged by the application. Which nmap scan type is BEST suited?
options: TCP Connect scan (-sT) — completes the full three-way handshake using the OS connect() syscall
FIN scan (-sF) — sends bare FIN packets and infers state from the lack of a RST response
ACK scan (-sA) — used to map firewall rule sets rather than determine open ports
SYN (half-open / stealth) scan (-sS) — sends SYN, reads SYN/ACK or RST, then tears the session down with RST
questions.explanation: An SYN (half-open) scan sends a SYN, reads the SYN/ACK or RST response to classify the port, then immediately sends a RST so the connection is never fully established — the application layer therefore does not log a session. It requires raw-socket privileges (root/Administrator). 'TCP Connect (-sT)' explicitly completes the handshake via connect(), which is exactly what the scenario tries to avoid. 'FIN scan (-sF)' is stealthier still but only works against strict RFC 793 stacks (most modern Windows hosts treat any non-SYN as closed and answer with RST regardless of port state, so it produces unreliable results). 'ACK scan (-sA)' does not determine open vs. closed — it maps whether a firewall is stateful by checking if the ACK is filtered, so it answers a different question.

questions.question: A red-team operator pulls WHOIS records, enumerates DNS, scrapes LinkedIn employee titles, and reviews the target's public GitHub repositories — without ever sending a packet directly to the target's production network. Which reconnaissance category is this?
options: Active footprinting — packets are sent directly to the target so banners and service versions can be enumerated
Vulnerability scanning — automated tools probe known CVEs against services running on the target hosts
Passive reconnaissance — information is gathered from third-party sources without sending traffic to the target itself
Social engineering — pretexting calls or phishing emails are used to elicit information directly from staff
questions.explanation: Passive reconnaissance gathers information from third-party sources (registries, search engines, public code, social media) without sending probes that would appear in the target's logs. The target sees no traffic, so detection is essentially impossible. 'Active footprinting' is the opposite — banner grabbing, traceroute, ping sweeps and similar techniques all touch the target. 'Vulnerability scanning' is a noisy active step (Nessus, OpenVAS) that fires CVE checks at the host. 'Social engineering' involves direct human interaction with employees and is also active because the attacker contacts the organization. Only the third-party-only collection in the scenario qualifies as passive.

questions.question: An attacker who has extracted NTLM hashes from a compromised Windows host re-authenticates to other servers using the raw hash, without ever cracking it to plaintext. Which underlying weakness makes a Pass-the-Hash attack possible?
options: Local Security Authority Subsystem Service caches the user's plaintext password indefinitely in process memory
NTLM authentication treats the password hash itself as the credential — the protocol never requires the plaintext to be presented
The SAM database stores account passwords using a reversible encryption that the attacker can decrypt with the boot key
Kerberos pre-authentication is downgraded to RC4-HMAC whenever a workstation joins a legacy domain
questions.explanation: In NTLM, the client proves knowledge of the password by encrypting a server-supplied challenge with a key derived from the password hash. The hash is therefore functionally equivalent to the password — anyone holding it can complete the challenge/response, so cracking it to plaintext is unnecessary. Mitigations are LAPS, restricted-admin / credential guard, tiered admin and disabling NTLM where possible. 'LSASS caches plaintext' is wrong on modern Windows: it caches credential material in a form usable for SSO, but Credential Guard isolates this and patched Windows does not retain reusable plaintext for interactive logons by default. 'SAM stores reversible encryption' is false — SAM stores LM/NTLM hashes (one-way), not reversible ciphertext. 'Kerberos downgrade to RC4' enables Kerberoasting/AS-REP attacks, which are distinct from PtH and do not rely on NTLM at all.
questions.domain: System Hacking Phases and Attack Techniques

questions.question: Malware loads a signed kernel-mode driver that hooks system-call tables so that specific processes, files and registry keys are invisible to user-mode tools such as Task Manager, dir and regedit. Which malware category does this BEST describe?
options: Kernel-mode rootkit — operates at ring 0 and modifies OS internals so its presence is hidden from user-mode utilities
Banking trojan — performs form-grabbing and webinjects in the browser to steal credentials at submission time
Crypto-ransomware — enumerates user files, encrypts them with a per-victim key and demands payment for the decryptor
Polymorphic worm — replicates across the network by mutating its payload to evade signature-based antivirus detection
questions.explanation: A kernel-mode (ring-0) rootkit installs itself inside the operating system kernel — typically as a driver — and intercepts system calls or directly manipulates kernel objects (DKOM) so that the artifacts it lists are filtered out before user-mode tools ever see them. Detection therefore requires booting from clean media, comparing offline file-system views, or using kernel-level integrity tooling such as PatchGuard / HVCI / Secure Boot. 'Banking trojan' steals credentials but does not hide kernel objects. 'Crypto-ransomware' is loud by design — it wants the victim to notice, so concealment is not its goal. 'Polymorphic worm' addresses signature evasion via payload mutation, but the hiding here is achieved through OS subversion, not by changing the binary's signature.
questions.domain: System Hacking Phases and Attack Techniques

questions.question: An attacker is plugged into a modern switched LAN and wants to capture traffic flowing between two other hosts on the same VLAN that they are not on the path of. Which technique enables this on commodity switches without special hardware?
options: Enabling promiscuous mode on the attacker's NIC so it accepts frames addressed to other MACs
Performing a DNS zone transfer (AXFR) against the segment's primary nameserver
Requesting that the switch mirror the relevant ports to the attacker via SPAN / port-mirroring
Poisoning the ARP caches of the two victims so each one resolves the other's IP to the attacker's MAC
questions.explanation: ARP spoofing inserts the attacker as a transparent man-in-the-middle: by sending unsolicited ARP replies, each victim caches the attacker's MAC for the other's IP, so the switch then forwards their frames to the attacker, who relays them after sniffing. Defences are Dynamic ARP Inspection, DHCP snooping bindings, and static ARP for critical hosts. 'Promiscuous mode' is necessary to read frames the NIC receives but a switch will not deliver other hosts' unicast frames to that port in the first place. 'DNS zone transfer' enumerates DNS records — useful for footprinting, but not a sniffing primitive on the LAN. 'SPAN / port-mirroring' would work, but it requires administrative access to the switch (the attacker normally does not have it) — the question asks how to do this on commodity switches without that level of access.

questions.question: A login form concatenates user input directly into the SQL statement without parameterization. The attacker enters the username `admin' --` and any password, and is logged in as admin. Which web-attack class is this and what is the precise mechanism?
options: Reflected cross-site scripting — the attacker's payload is echoed back into the response and executes in the victim's browser
In-band SQL injection (authentication bypass via comment) — the `--` comments out the rest of the WHERE clause, including the password check
Cross-site request forgery — the victim's authenticated browser is tricked into submitting a state-changing request to the application
LDAP injection — operators such as `*)(&` are injected into a directory-search filter to broaden the result set
questions.explanation: Concatenating untrusted input into SQL is the textbook SQL-injection class. The single quote closes the username literal and the `--` comments out everything after it on that line — so the WHERE clause becomes `WHERE username='admin'`, the password test is dropped, and the application authenticates the attacker as admin. This is an in-band (classic / tautology) SQLi used for authentication bypass. Parameterized queries / prepared statements remove the attack surface entirely. 'Reflected XSS' injects script into a rendered response, not into a SQL statement. 'CSRF' rides an already-authenticated session — it does not bypass authentication. 'LDAP injection' uses LDAP filter metacharacters (`*`, `(`, `)`, `&`, `|`) against a directory server, not SQL.

questions.question: A single-page application reads its hash fragment via `location.hash` and writes it straight into `innerHTML`. An attacker shares a link of the form `https://app.example/#`. The payload never reaches the server. Which XSS variant is this?
options: Reflected (Type-I) XSS — the payload travels through the server in a query parameter and is reflected back into the rendered HTML response
Stored (Type-II) XSS — the payload is persisted in a database or filesystem and served back to any later visitor
DOM-based (Type-0) XSS — the malicious data flows from a client-side source into a client-side sink without ever leaving the browser
Blind XSS — the payload fires only inside an administrative interface that the attacker themselves cannot directly observe
questions.explanation: DOM-based XSS occurs entirely client-side: a script reads attacker-controlled data from a DOM source (here `location.hash`) and passes it to a dangerous DOM sink (here `innerHTML`) without the server ever seeing the payload — browser fragments are not sent in HTTP requests. The fix is to use safe sinks (`textContent`, framework-bound templates) or contextual escaping such as DOMPurify. 'Reflected XSS' would require the server to echo the payload back in its response, which does not happen with a fragment. 'Stored XSS' would require persistence on the server. 'Blind XSS' describes WHERE the payload eventually fires (in an admin console invisible to the attacker), not how it is delivered — and the question is about delivery mechanics.

questions.question: WPA2-Personal is vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks against captured four-way handshakes (and the PMKID variant against single beacons). Which specific WPA3-Personal mechanism makes that offline cracking infeasible?
options: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE / Dragonfly) — a password-authenticated key exchange that requires an online guess per attempt and provides forward secrecy
Mandatory 192-bit Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite — required for every WPA3-Personal client and AP regardless of deployment
Static rotation of the GTK (Group Temporal Key) every 60 seconds, derived from the pre-shared key with no client interaction
Caching of the PMKID inside Beacon and Probe-Response frames so roaming clients can re-associate without re-authenticating
questions.explanation: SAE (a.k.a. Dragonfly) is a password-authenticated key exchange: each guess at the password requires a full online handshake with the AP, so capturing frames and cracking offline at GPU speeds — the entire WPA2 PSK attack model — stops working. SAE also provides forward secrecy, so even a future password disclosure does not decrypt previously captured sessions. The 192-bit CNSA suite is associated with WPA3-Enterprise, not Personal — calling it 'mandatory for every WPA3 client' is wrong. Periodic GTK rotation existed in WPA2 and is unrelated to PSK offline cracking. PMKID caching in Beacons/Probe-Responses is precisely the WPA2 weakness Jens Steube exploited; WPA3 does not advertise PMKID this way.

questions.question: An attacker sends small DNS queries with the victim's IP spoofed as the source to a list of open recursive resolvers. The resolvers reply to the victim with much larger responses, saturating the victim's link. Which two characteristics of this attack are the primary enablers?
options: Recursive resolvers always answer queries received on TCP port 53 only, which simplifies routing to the spoofed victim
Modern resolvers transparently compress responses so that signature-based volumetric defences see only the small inbound query
DNSSEC signatures encrypt the payload end-to-end, preventing intermediate networks from rate-limiting amplified traffic
DNS responses are several times larger than the corresponding queries (a high amplification factor) and the UDP source address can be spoofed
questions.explanation: DNS reflection/amplification rests on two facts: (1) DNS over UDP allows the source IP to be spoofed so the response goes to the victim instead of the attacker, and (2) the response (especially for ANY, large TXT or DNSSEC-signed zones) is many times larger than the query — amplification factors of 30× or more are routine — so the attacker spends a fraction of the bandwidth the victim has to absorb. Mitigations: BCP 38 ingress filtering, closing open resolvers, response-rate limiting, anycast scrubbing. The other options are incorrect: DNS is primarily UDP/53 (not TCP-only), there is no transparent compression that defeats volumetric defences, and DNSSEC signs but does not encrypt — it actually makes responses LARGER, which makes amplification worse, not better.

questions.question: A pentester recovers a database of unsalted MD5 password hashes and cracks 70% of them in minutes using a precomputed rainbow table. Which defensive change at the application layer would have made this specific attack effectively useless?
options: Switching the storage algorithm from MD5 to SHA-1 while keeping the hashes unsalted
Generating a unique random salt per password and storing it alongside the hash, ideally combined with a memory-hard KDF such as bcrypt / Argon2
Wrapping each stored hash with AES-128 encryption using a key kept inside the same database server
Truncating the resulting hash to 64 bits so that fewer characters need to be presented at login time
questions.explanation: A unique random salt per password makes every hash unique even when users pick the same password, which renders precomputed tables (rainbow tables, lookup tables) useless — an attacker would need to build one table per salt, defeating the precomputation. Pairing the salt with a memory-hard KDF (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2id) additionally slows each guess by orders of magnitude. 'SHA-1 unsalted' just swaps one fast unsalted hash for another and is itself broken — rainbow tables exist for SHA-1 as well. 'AES-wrap with a key on the same server' fails the assumed threat model: if the attacker dumped the hashes, they almost certainly also have the key. 'Truncate to 64 bits' makes brute force EASIER (smaller search space) and increases collisions; it is the opposite of what is needed.

questions.question: A pentester discovers that a corporate AWS S3 bucket containing customer invoices has been left with a public-read bucket ACL and `s3:GetObject` allowed in its policy for `Principal: "*"`. Which cloud-attack category from the CEH v12 cloud module BEST describes the underlying issue?
options: Cloud misconfiguration — specifically, an object-storage exposure caused by an over-permissive ACL / bucket policy granting public read
Virtual-machine / hypervisor escape — a guest workload breaks out of its VM and reads the host's memory
Container breakout — a process inside an unprivileged container escapes the namespace and gains code execution on the node
SaaS API token theft — an OAuth refresh token is exfiltrated from a developer's machine and replayed against the SaaS provider
questions.explanation: Cloud misconfiguration — over-permissive identity, network and storage settings — is consistently the leading cause of cloud breaches (cited in every major cloud-security report) and is treated as its own threat in the CEH v12 cloud module. Publicly readable S3 buckets are the canonical example: scanning the public IPv4 space and S3 namespaces for `200 OK` GETs reliably surfaces sensitive data left in misconfigured tenants. Controls: AWS Block Public Access at account and bucket level, IAM Access Analyzer, and CSPM/SSPM tooling. 'Hypervisor escape' and 'container breakout' are isolation failures inside the compute plane and unrelated to bucket ACLs. 'SaaS API token theft' is a credential-exfiltration issue against a SaaS provider, not an IaaS storage exposure.

questions.question: An IP camera ships with a fixed Telnet account `root / xc3511` documented in its service manual and not changeable through the web UI. The Mirai botnet famously enrolled hundreds of thousands of similar devices. Which OWASP IoT / CEH v12 IoT threat does this exemplify?
options: Lack of a secure firmware-update mechanism — devices cannot receive signed patches once shipped
Insecure data transfer and storage — the device transmits telemetry over an unauthenticated cleartext channel
Use of weak, guessable or hard-coded credentials — accounts are pre-set, identical across units and cannot be rotated by the owner
Insecure ecosystem interfaces — the companion mobile or web app exposes IDOR-style endpoints that authorize horizontally
questions.explanation: Hard-coded, vendor-set credentials that the owner cannot rotate is the textbook example of OWASP IoT Top 10 #1 — 'Weak, Guessable or Hard-coded Passwords' — and is also the exact vector Mirai used: a small list of factory default Telnet/SSH logins enrolled hundreds of thousands of cameras and DVRs into a DDoS botnet. The fix is to require unique per-device credentials at first boot and to disable obsolete management protocols (Telnet) outright. 'Lack of secure update' (OWASP IoT #4) prevents fielded fixes but is not what enables the initial compromise here. 'Insecure data transfer and storage' is about TLS / encryption-at-rest, not about login credentials. 'Insecure ecosystem interfaces' covers the companion app/cloud-API tier, which is downstream of the device-credential issue described.
questions.domain: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking

questions.question: A red team has a low-privilege shell on a Windows host and recovers the local SAM. Rather than cracking the NTLM hashes offline, the operator wants to authenticate to other hosts that share the local admin password. Which technique fits, and what control most directly defeats it?
options: Pass-the-Hash using the NTLM hash directly against SMB; defeated by enforcing unique local admin passwords via LAPS and enabling SMB signing.
Kerberoasting the service accounts; defeated by rotating the KRBTGT key twice.
Golden Ticket forgery; defeated by shortening the maximum ticket lifetime.
LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning; defeated by deploying a WSUS server.
questions.explanation: NTLM authentication proves knowledge of the hash, not the plaintext, so a captured hash can be replayed directly (Pass-the-Hash) without cracking. When every workstation shares the same local Administrator password, one hash unlocks the fleet — Microsoft LAPS randomizes each machine's local admin password to break that lateral path, and SMB signing hardens the session. Kerberoasting targets service-account TGS tickets (a different attack against domain SPNs). A Golden Ticket requires the KRBTGT hash, which a local SAM does not contain. LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning is a name-resolution capture technique, unrelated to replaying a recovered SAM hash.
questions.domain: System Hacking Phases and Attack Techniques

questions.question: During enumeration of an internal network, a tester runs `snmpwalk` against a router using the community string 'public' and receives the full interface and routing table. Which finding and remediation are correct?
options: The router is running SNMPv3 with authPriv; no action needed because traffic is encrypted.
A default read-only community string is exposing device data; remediate by removing default strings and moving to SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption.
This is a DNS zone transfer; remediate by restricting AXFR to secondaries.
This is an SMB null session; remediate by disabling anonymous IPC$ access.
questions.explanation: A successful `snmpwalk` with the community string 'public' proves the device still uses a default SNMPv1/v2c read-only string, which leaks interface, routing, and system data in cleartext. The fix is to remove default/guessable community strings and migrate to SNMPv3, which adds user authentication and payload encryption (authPriv). If it were truly SNMPv3 authPriv, the walk would have failed without credentials. Zone transfers (AXFR) and SMB null sessions are entirely different enumeration vectors and would not be driven by an SNMP community string.

questions.question: A web app sets its session cookie without the HttpOnly and Secure flags, and reflects unsanitized input into the page. An attacker wants to steal live sessions at scale. Which chained attack is MOST effective and which single cookie flag would blunt the theft step?
options: CSRF to change the victim's password; the SameSite flag stops it.
SQL injection to dump the session table; the Secure flag stops it.
Reflected/stored XSS that reads document.cookie and exfiltrates it; the HttpOnly flag stops the cookie read.
Clickjacking via an invisible iframe; the HttpOnly flag stops it.
questions.explanation: Unsanitized reflected input plus a script-readable cookie is the classic XSS-to-session-hijack chain: injected JavaScript reads `document.cookie` and sends it to an attacker endpoint. Setting HttpOnly removes the cookie from the DOM/JavaScript scope, so even a successful XSS payload cannot read it. The Secure flag only forces HTTPS transport (it does not stop a script read), SameSite mitigates cross-site request forgery rather than script-based theft, and SQL injection against a session table is not what the reflected-input weakness enables here.

questions.question: A tester captures the WPA2-PSK 4-way handshake for a target SSID and wants to recover the passphrase offline. Which statement about the attack is accurate?
options: The handshake lets you decrypt all past traffic immediately without knowing the passphrase, because the PMK is transmitted in frame 2.
The attack only works if WPS is enabled, because the PSK is derived from the WPS PIN.
Capturing the handshake is unnecessary; WPA2-PSK keys can always be read from the beacon frames.
You must perform an offline dictionary/brute-force attack: the handshake enables verifying candidate passphrases against the captured MIC, so a strong passphrase defeats it.
questions.explanation: The WPA2-PSK 4-way handshake never transmits the PSK or PMK; it exchanges nonces and a MIC. Capturing it lets an attacker test candidate passphrases offline — derive the PMK from a guess plus the SSID, compute the PTK and MIC, and compare to the captured MIC. This makes passphrase strength the whole defense: a long, random passphrase is computationally infeasible to brute-force. The PMK is not sent in frame 2, keys are not present in beacons, and while a separate WPS PIN attack exists, WPA2-PSK cracking via handshake capture does not depend on WPS.

questions.question: A phishing email passes SPF because it was sent through a permitted relay, yet it spoofs the display name and From header of the CEO. Which email-authentication control is designed to catch this specific gap?
options: DMARC with alignment between the visible From domain and an authenticated SPF or DKIM identity.
DKIM alone, because it encrypts the message body end to end.
STARTTLS, because it authenticates the sending user.
Greylisting, because it blocks all first-time senders permanently.
questions.explanation: SPF validates the envelope (Return-Path) domain, not the header From that users see, so mail relayed through an allowed server can still spoof the visible From. DMARC closes this by requiring 'alignment' — the header From domain must match a domain that passed SPF or DKIM — and it publishes a policy (none/quarantine/reject) telling receivers what to do on failure. DKIM signs (not encrypts) the message and by itself does not enforce From alignment. STARTTLS only encrypts transport, and greylisting is an anti-spam delay tactic, not a spoofing control.

questions.question: An attacker on the same subnet as a target sends a stream of gratuitous ARP replies mapping the default gateway's IP to the attacker's MAC. What is the immediate effect, and which control most directly prevents it on a managed switch?
options: It exhausts the DHCP pool (starvation); prevented by port security limiting MAC counts.
It poisons victims' ARP caches so their gateway-bound traffic flows through the attacker (MITM); prevented by Dynamic ARP Inspection tied to DHCP snooping.
It floods the CAM table so the switch fails open; prevented by BPDU guard.
It performs a SYN flood against the gateway; prevented by SYN cookies.
questions.explanation: Unsolicited (gratuitous) ARP replies overwrite the victims' cached IP-to-MAC mapping for the gateway, so their outbound traffic is sent to the attacker — a classic ARP-poisoning man-in-the-middle. Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP packets against the DHCP snooping binding table and drops forged mappings, which directly stops it. DHCP starvation, CAM-table flooding, and SYN floods are separate attacks; port security, BPDU guard, and SYN cookies address those other cases, not ARP cache poisoning.

questions.question: A tester finds a parameter that fetches a URL supplied by the client so the server can pull a preview image. They make the server request `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`. Which vulnerability class is this, and what is the primary risk on a cloud host?
options: Local File Inclusion (LFI); it reads /etc/passwd from the web root.
Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF); it forces the victim's browser to submit a form.
Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF); it can reach the instance metadata service and expose temporary cloud credentials.
Open redirect; it only sends the user to an attacker page.
questions.explanation: When a server fetches an attacker-controlled URL, the attacker can pivot the server's trust to reach internal endpoints — the hallmark of SSRF. On many cloud instances the link-local metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) returns instance role credentials, so an unguarded fetch can leak temporary keys and escalate into the cloud account (the reason IMDSv2 and egress controls exist). CSRF abuses a victim's browser, LFI reads local files via path traversal, and an open redirect merely bounces a user — none of which describe the server itself making an internal request.

questions.question: An organization asks whether MD5 is acceptable for storing user passwords. As the ethical hacker, which recommendation is correct and why?
options: MD5 is fine if each password is salted, because salting makes MD5 collision-resistant.
Encrypt passwords with AES-256 so they can be decrypted and re-hashed later.
Switch to SHA-256 without a salt, since a longer digest alone stops rainbow tables.
MD5 is unacceptable for passwords; use a slow, salted, purpose-built KDF such as bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 to resist GPU brute-forcing.
questions.explanation: MD5 is extremely fast and thus ideal for attackers — modern GPUs test billions of MD5 guesses per second — and salting only defeats precomputed rainbow tables, not fast brute-forcing. Password storage should use a deliberately slow, memory-hard KDF (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) with a per-user salt and a tunable work factor. Plain SHA-256 is still fast even with a salt, and reversibly encrypting passwords with AES is an anti-pattern because a key compromise exposes every plaintext at once.

questions.question: A team wants to detect attackers early and gather intelligence on their techniques without exposing production systems. They deploy a decoy host with fake services and heavy logging, isolated from the real network. What is this called, and what is its main legal/operational caution?
options: A honeypot; caution: it must be isolated and closely monitored so it cannot be used as a pivot into production.
A jump box; caution: it must never be patched.
A bastion CA; caution: it must issue only wildcard certificates.
A WAF; caution: it must run in monitor-only mode forever.
questions.explanation: A decoy system with fake services, designed to attract and observe attackers, is a honeypot. Its value is early detection and technique intelligence, but the key caution is containment: a compromised honeypot must not become a launch point into real assets, so it is network-isolated and closely monitored, and organizations should confirm legal/entrapment considerations. A jump box/bastion is an administrative access host, a CA issues certificates, and a WAF filters web traffic — none match a monitored decoy.
questions.domain: System Hacking Phases and Attack Techniques

questions.question: A scan of a container host reveals the Docker Engine API listening on TCP 2375 with no TLS and no authentication, reachable from the network. Why is this critical, and what is the correct fix?
options: It is low risk because the API only reports read-only container stats; fix by renaming the daemon.
It lets anyone who can reach the port create privileged containers and mount the host filesystem; fix by never exposing 2375 and requiring mutual TLS on 2376 or a local socket.
It only affects image pulls from Docker Hub; fix by using a private registry.
It is a false positive because Docker never listens on TCP; fix by ignoring it.
questions.explanation: An unauthenticated, unencrypted Docker API on 2375 gives full control of the daemon to anyone who can reach it. An attacker can launch a privileged container that bind-mounts the host root filesystem, yielding root on the underlying host and every other container. The remediation is to never expose the plaintext port — bind the daemon to a local Unix socket, or if remote access is required, enable mutually authenticated TLS on 2376. The API is far more than read-only, Docker can indeed listen on TCP, and the risk is unrelated to registry choice.
